## Equivalence of Definitions of Adjunction

We wish to demonstrate that the two definitions of an adjunction are equivalent.

### Definition 1 implies Definition 2

Assume Definition 1 holds. Then we have a natural isomorphism $\alpha: \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-, -) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-, G-)$ between the two hom-bifunctors from $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$ to $\mathbf{Set}$.

By the definition of a natural isomorphism, its components are isomorphisms in the target category. Since the target category is $\mathbf{Set}$, the isomorphisms are exactly bijections. Therefore, for every object $\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$, the component 
$$ \alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}} : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD, C) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D, GC) $$
is a bijection. This establishes the family of bijections required by Definition 2.

Furthermore, by the definition of a natural transformation, $\alpha$ satisfies a naturality condition for any morphism in the domain category. Consider an arbitrary morphism $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g} : \tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1} \to \tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$. This corresponds to a morphism $f: D_2 \to D_1$ in $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $g: C_1 \to C_2$ in $\mathbf C$.

The naturality of $\alpha$ asserts that the following diagram commutes:
$$ \alpha_{\tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}} \circ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg) \circ \alpha_{\tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1}} $$
where the actions of the bifunctors on the morphism $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$ are given by:
* $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g)(h) = g \circ h \circ Ff$ for any $h \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD_1, C_1)$
* $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg)(h) = Gg \circ h \circ f$ for any $h \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D_1, GC_1)$

This commutative square is precisely the commutative diagram detailed in Definition 2. Thus, Definition 2 holds.

### Definition 2 implies Definition 1

Conversely, assume Definition 2 holds. We are given a family of bijections $\alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}}$ that satisfy the commutative diagram:
$$ \alpha_{\tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}} \circ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg) \circ \alpha_{\tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1}} $$
for all objects and all morphisms $f^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $g$.

The commutativity of this diagram for all morphisms $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$ is exactly the definition of $\alpha$ being a natural transformation between the bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-, -)$ and the bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-, G-)$.

Because each component $\alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}}$ is given to be a bijection, every component of the natural transformation is an isomorphism in $\mathbf{Set}$. A natural transformation whose components are all isomorphisms is, by definition, a natural isomorphism.

Therefore, $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism between $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-, -)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-, G-)$, which precisely satisfies Definition 1.

Since both implications hold, the two definitions are logically equivalent.
